name: Val d'Arno di Sopra

climate: Seasons this warm ripen Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon, Sangiovese, Chardonnay and Sauvignon Blanc fully without cooking off their freshness.
Sangiovese, Merlot and Cabernet Sauvignon sit in their sweet spot, so the wines can show the style they are known for.

soil.rock: Limestone makes alkaline soil that drains well yet can hold water for the vines. It is usually planted to grapes valued for their acidity. Shale and mudstone are fine-grained rocks that hold heat well and are moderately fertile.
soil.top: The topsoil holds water well and drains at a steady pace, so vines rarely go thirsty or sit in wet ground. Its high pH can starve vines of iron and yellow the leaves, so growers plant lime-tolerant rootstocks.

land: The high ground runs about 6°F cooler than the low ground. Higher vineyards ripen later and keep more acidity, so one grape can make lighter or richer wine here depending on height.
Much of it is steep. Cold air and rain run off, so frost and waterlogging are rare and soils stay thin, keeping yields low. Steep rows are slow and costly to work, often by hand.

winkler: Early and mid-season grapes make good wine.

sheet.place: Val d'Arno di Sopra is a DOC in the upper Arno valley, between Arezzo and Florence. It dates from 2011 and grew out of the older Pietraviva DOC. The red blend is Merlot-led.

claims.claim: Val d'Arno di Sopra (also written Valdarno di Sopra) was approved as a DOC by ministerial decree of 13 June 2011 (Gazzetta Ufficiale 148, 28 June 2011). It was changed in 2011, 2014 and, with a large rewrite, in 2024.

Pietraviva came first. In 2001 a group of producers (Petrolo, Villa La Selva, I Selvatici) asked the government for a Pietraviva DOC for the west side of the valley, next to Chianti Classico. It was granted around 2005 and merged into Val d'Arno di Sopra in 2011.

The producers first wanted the DOC called Valdarno Superiore, which would have covered both sides of the valley. A nearby cooperative that uses that name objected, so they chose Pietraviva. No source explains the word Pietraviva itself.

From 2011 until the 2024 rewrite the DOC had two subzones, Pietraviva and Pratomagno. In the 2011 text Pietraviva covered Cavriglia, Montevarchi, Bucine, San Giovanni Valdarno, Pergine Valdarno and Civitella in Val di Chiana.

The 2024 consolidated disciplinare has no subzones. Pietraviva appears only in the history section, as the earlier DOC on which Valdarno di Sopra was built. Petrolo says producers proposed dropping the two subzones.

The DOC zone is the entire territory of Cavriglia, Montevarchi, Bucine, Civitella in Val di Chiana, Castelfranco-Piandisco, Terranuova Bracciolini, Loro Ciuffenna, San Giovanni Valdarno, Castiglion Fibocchi and Laterina-Pergine Valdarno. It also includes the part of Arezzo comune between Civitella, Laterina-Pergine and Castiglion Fibocchi and the Canale Maestro della Chiana and Arno, up to the Capolona border. In the province of Florence it takes in all of Figline e Incisa Valdarno, Reggello and Rignano sull'Arno.

The zone lies on both sides of the Arno valley, between the Arezzo plain and the Florentine hills. The disciplinare places it roughly between the Casentino and Chianti, and says a 1716 decree of Grand Duke Cosimo III de' Medici defined the Valdarno as a quality wine area.

Rosso: Merlot 40 to 80%, with Sangiovese and/or Cabernet Sauvignon and/or Syrah and/or Cabernet Franc up to 50%, and other red grapes up to 30%. Bianco: Chardonnay 40 to 80%, with Trebbiano Toscano and/or Malvasia Bianca Lunga up to 50%, Sauvignon up to 10%, and other whites up to 30%.

Single-variety wines need at least 85% of that grape. The named varieties are Chardonnay, Sauvignon, Malvasia Bianca Lunga, Orpicchio, Trebbiano, Sangiovese, Cabernet Sauvignon, Cabernet Franc, Merlot, Syrah, Malvasia Nera, Canaiolo Nero, Ciliegiolo, Pinot Nero, Pugnitello and Foglia Tonda. Sangiovese, Cabernet Franc and Pugnitello can also be made as rosato.

The DOC also covers a rosato sparkling wine from at least 85% Sangiovese, made by the traditional method with 48 months on the lees. Vin Santo (Malvasia Bianca Lunga and/or Trebbiano) and Vin Santo Occhio di Pernice (Sangiovese at least 80%) are also allowed, along with late harvest white and red.

Red riserva needs 24 months from 1 November of the harvest year, with at least 12 in wood and 3 in bottle. White riserva needs 12 months, with 6 in wood and 3 in bottle. Plain red cannot be sold before 31 March of the year after the harvest. Whites and rosati cannot be sold before 1 February.

The maximum yield is 11 t/ha for all types. The wine yield is capped at 70%. Natural alcohol is 12.0% for most reds (13.0% for riserva) and 11.5% for whites. New plantings need at least 4,100 vines per hectare.
Vineyards below 170 m above sea level are excluded from the register. The rules set no top limit.
The main vineyard exposure is west to south-west. This gives well ventilated, bright sites. The disciplinare says growers favour soils with good texture and depth.

A zoning study by the University of Milan (Scienza) found the foothill and alluvial bands of the DOC fairly uniform. The ridges are formed from the lower Miocene Tuscan series. The Macigno formation is turbiditic quartz-feldspar sandstone with a little calcite, alternating with silty schists. The Londa formation is mostly silty schists with some marl, fine sandstone and limestone.
A working group of local growers and winemakers says the geology gives the wines a savoury, mineral character whatever the grape. The disciplinare also says the reds show 'mountain fruit' notes.

Climate: temperate-cold for much of the year, with Mediterranean influence in summer that helps ripening. Winters are cold and hard, summers hot and sunny, with strong temperature swings. The area falls in an intermediate class on the Rocchi and Pastena scale, where negative climate traits are weak.
Average rainfall is 550 to 900 mm a year depending on the year, about 70% of it in autumn and winter.

A large day to night swing in summer helps the wines keep their aromas, according to the disciplinare. It says the whites are intense and persistent, thanks to the warm to cold alternation of the foothill climate.

The disciplinare traces wine here to the Etruscans and Pliny the Elder, and to the 1427 Florentine Catasto, which graded wines by quality. From the 1970s some producers made wines of high standing as IGT, which led to Pietraviva and then Valdarno di Sopra.
In 1716 Cosimo III named four areas whose wines could be exported with the origin shown: Chianti Classico, Pomino, Carmignano and Val d'Arno di Sopra.

In 2001 Wine Spectator said the area was making a handful of top-ranked wines, naming Petrolo's Torrione and Galatrona and Villa La Selva's Selvamaggio and Felciaia. The proposed Pietraviva area was about 2,500 acres.
Val d'Arno di Sopra means the upper part of the Arno valley, the stretch between Arezzo and Florence. Di Sopra means upper, as in upstream.

gaps: The 2011 disciplinare could not be opened. The Pietraviva commune list and the Pratomagno list rest on search summaries. The Pratomagno list is incomplete.
No source explains the word Pietraviva.
No altitude figures beyond the 170 m minimum, and no soil detail by commune.
No independent climate data (temperature, growing degree days) for the upper Arno valley.
The 2024 rewrite: only the final text was read. The reasons for dropping subzones were not found.
